name: Exosome serums

lead: Exosome serums contain extracellular vesicles, tiny particles cells release to signal each other. They are used for skin regeneration and rejuvenation, often after microneedling, to speed recovery and improve texture.

Vesicles carry proteins, lipids and RNA between cells, and the idea is that these signals prompt skin cells to repair and renew. Extracellular vesicles are an active research area, but a couple of registered trials turned up with no published results for cosmetic use.

paras: Applied as a serum, most often right after microneedling or other procedures, as part of a recovery and rejuvenation routine.

Researchers note that isolating and measuring vesicles is difficult and standardization is lacking, so products vary. No regulatory or adverse-event data for cosmetic products were in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Exosome serums carry cell signals meant to drive skin repair, applied after microneedling for faster recovery and smoother, rejuvenated skin. The biology is active in the lab, and published human skin data are very limited.

lead: Exosome serums are skincare and post-procedure products marketed as containing exosomes or other extracellular vesicles, small membrane-enclosed particles that cells release.[1] They are promoted for regeneration and rejuvenation, often alongside procedures such as microneedling.

Extracellular vesicles are an active research area, but in the sources reviewed the evidence for cosmetic products is limited to a small number of registered trials. Researchers have noted that isolating and measuring vesicles is difficult and standardization is lacking.[1]

paras: Extracellular vesicles are released by nearly all cell types; most are under about 200 nm. Some bud from the cell surface, while exosomes form inside cells and are released when multivesicular bodies fuse with the membrane. They can carry proteins, lipids, RNA and other molecules, and are thought to pass signals between cells.[1]

Wikipedia's overview also lists proposed risks of vesicles in biology, including effects on clotting and the spread of inflammation, and notes that tumor-derived vesicles can promote cancer invasion; these concern vesicles in the body rather than cosmetic products specifically.[1]

Few trials appear in the sources reviewed. One completed, 30-participant study registered in 2024 tested AnteAGE Biosomes with radiofrequency microneedling for facial rejuvenation, with skin aging, wrinkles and skin tone as listed conditions; no results are given in the registration entry reviewed.[2] A separate registered phase 2 acne trial concerns skin microbiome balance and is listed here without published results.[3] No published efficacy results for exosome serums were found.

Standardization remains a major gap in vesicle science, and contamination by non-vesicle material has been a persistent problem in isolation.[1] The sources reviewed do not include regulatory statements on cosmetic exosome products.
